lessons.title: How Working Capital Affects Profitability, Growth and Valuation

children.text: Working capital has been a cash management topic for six chapters. It is also a profitability topic, a growth topic and a valuation topic, and this lesson connects the three.

The connection is mechanical, not philosophical. Working capital sits in the denominator of return on capital, it consumes the cash that funds growth, and its year-on-year movement enters free cash flow directly. Move it and all three change.

body.caption: Two companies with identical profit can report very different returns

children.text: Two companies each do ₹500 crore of sales and earn ₹60 crore of operating profit on ₹150 crore of fixed capital. The only difference is that Company A runs working capital at 30% of sales and Company B at 15%.

Company B earns 6.7 percentage points more on the same profit, entirely because it has ₹75 crore less parked in stock and receivables. No pricing change, no cost cutting, no new product. This is the arithmetic behind the policy lesson in Chapter 3, now expressed as a competitive gap.

body.title: Find the ROCE
body.prompt: Using the same figures, sales of ₹500 crore, operating profit of ₹60 crore and fixed capital of ₹150 crore, what is the ROCE if working capital runs at 25% of sales? Give your answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Working capital is 25% of ₹500 crore, which is ₹125 crore. Capital employed is ₹275 crore, so ROCE is ₹60 crore divided by that, or 21.8%. Every five percentage points of working capital intensity is worth roughly one to two points of ROCE at this scale.

children.text: Growth: How Fast You Can Go Without Raising Money

Chapter 1 showed that growth consumes cash. Here is the formula behind it. If each rupee of new sales needs a fixed amount of working capital and capital expenditure, then retained profit sets a ceiling on how fast the business can grow without outside funding.

body.caption: The self-funded growth rate: how fast the business can grow on its own money

children.text: Both companies retain ₹45 crore of profit after tax, and both need about 10 paise of capital expenditure per rupee of new sales. Company A also needs 30 paise of working capital per rupee, Company B only 15.

body.label: The growth gap
body.context: Company B can grow 13.5 percentage points a year faster than Company A on identical profits, purely because each rupee of new sales absorbs less working capital.

body.text: This is the strategic argument for working capital discipline, and it is much stronger than the cost saving. A leaner cycle does not just improve returns, it raises the speed limit on growth. Two competitors with the same margin will separate over five years if one can self-fund 36% growth and the other stalls at 22.5% or has to keep raising money.

children.text: Valuation: Where the Money Actually Shows Up

body.caption: An increase in working capital is a direct subtraction from free cash flow

children.text: Take Company A in a growth year: operating profit after tax of ₹45 crore, depreciation of ₹18 crore, capital expenditure of ₹25 crore and a working capital increase of ₹38 crore.
is exactly ₹0 crore. A profitable, growing, well-run company generates nothing for its owners that year.

markDefs.definition: Free cash flow. What is left after funding operations, working capital and capital expenditure, and the number that drives valuation.

children.text: Halve the working capital increase to ₹19 crore and free cash flow becomes ₹19 crore. Nothing changed in the profit and loss statement. In a discounted cash flow valuation, that difference repeats every year and compounds into a materially different value.

body.title: How a permanent improvement creates value, in two parts

children.text: The one-time release. Cutting the cycle by 10 days on ₹500 crore of sales frees about ₹13.7 crore immediately, once. It behaves like a special dividend: it can repay debt, fund capital expenditure or be returned to shareholders, and it saves about ₹1.37 crore a year of interest at a 10% cost of funds.

The ongoing effect, which is larger. A lower working capital intensity means every future rupee of sales growth absorbs less cash, so free cash flow rises in every forecast year, not just the first. In a discounted cash flow model this shifts the whole projection, which is why analysts treat a sustained improvement in the cycle very differently from a one-off collection push before the year end.

A caution on multiples. Valuations quoted on enterprise value to EBITDA do not see working capital at all, because EBITDA is calculated before it. The working capital shows up in net debt, which is deducted to get equity value. Two companies on the same multiple can therefore be worth very different amounts to a buyer, and this is exactly what acquirers examine in diligence when they set a normalised working capital level in the purchase agreement.
There is a single ratio that tells you whether reported profit is arriving as cash: operating cash flow divided by operating profit.

body.text: Do not over-read a single year of this ratio. Cash conversion swings with one-off movements, tax timing and seasonality, and a single year proves nothing. What matters is the pattern: a company whose conversion sits below 70% year after year while profits grow is funding its profit growth with working capital, and that shows up eventually in borrowings.

body.title: Two companies reporting the same profit growth

columns.label: Earnings you can bank
points: Cash conversion consistently near or above 80%
Working capital growing no faster than sales
Receivables ageing stable, with the current bucket holding its share
Borrowings flat or falling while profit rises
Free cash flow positive across the cycle, not just in good years

columns.label: Earnings that live on the balance sheet
points: Working capital growing faster than sales, year after year
Receivables ageing deteriorating, with older buckets expanding
Free cash flow negative even in years without major capital expenditure

body.title: Where did the profit go?
body.question: A company reports 20% profit growth for the third year running, but its operating cash flow has been roughly flat and short-term borrowings have risen every year. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The company is investing heavily in new plant
Profit growth is being absorbed by rising working capital, most likely receivables and inventory
body.explanation: Capital expenditure would show in investing activities, not in operating cash flow. Flat operating cash flow alongside rising profit points to working capital absorbing the difference, and the rising short-term borrowing is how it is being funded. The next step is to check receivable and inventory days over the same three years.

body.title: The valuation link
body.textWithBlank: In a free cash flow calculation, an increase in working capital is ___ from operating profit after tax, which is why a profitable growing company can generate no free cash flow at all.
body.explanation: Free cash flow is operating profit after tax plus depreciation, less capital expenditure and less the increase in working capital. The working capital movement is a direct subtraction, and in a fast-growing business it can consume the entire profit.

body.title: The buyer who reads the balance sheet
body.scenario: You are advising the founders of a ₹400 crore packaging business who are in discussions to sell a majority stake. Their adviser has quoted a valuation of 10 times EBITDA of ₹48 crore, so ₹480 crore of enterprise value. The company runs working capital at 34% of sales, against a peer average closer to 20%, and has ₹95 crore of short-term borrowing funding it. The buyer has begun diligence.
body.prompt: What will the buyer do with the working capital position, and what should the founders do before the next meeting?
body.modelAnswer:
Expect the buyer to attack it from two directions, both legitimate.

First, net debt. Enterprise value of ₹480 crore less ₹95 crore of borrowing leaves ₹385 crore of equity value, before anything else. The founders may be anchored on ₹480 crore, but the working capital funded by that debt is already subtracting from what they receive.

Second, the normalised working capital mechanism. Purchase agreements typically fix a normal level of working capital, with the price adjusted for any shortfall or excess at completion. A buyer looking at 34% of sales against a peer norm nearer 20% will argue that roughly ₹56 crore is excess working capital, and will either treat it as an adjustment or price the business assuming it must be funded. This is where most of the value gap in mid-market Indian deals actually appears, and it is rarely the headline multiple.

What the founders should do before the next meeting. Diagnose the 34% honestly, using the tools from Chapters 2 and 4: how much is genuinely required by the business model, how much is old receivables and slow-moving stock, and how much is habit. If a realistic path takes the business to 26% or 27% within a year, that is roughly ₹28 crore of cash and a materially better negotiating position, and it is far more persuasive presented as a plan with named owners than as an assurance.

And a timing point worth saying plainly: improvements made before diligence belong to the seller, while improvements identified during diligence belong to the buyer. The work has more value now than it will in three months.

body.title: Link working capital to the numbers the board cares about
steps: Report working capital as a percentage of sales alongside ROCE every quarter, not just in rupees.
Compute the self-funded growth rate and compare it with the growth plan, since a gap means new funding is required.
Track the cash conversion ratio over five years and investigate any sustained level below 70%.
Convert every proposed improvement in days into a one-time cash release and an ongoing interest saving.
In any valuation discussion, separate the headline multiple from net debt and the normalised working capital adjustment.
When analysing another company, read cash conversion, working capital intensity and borrowings together rather than separately.
Treat a sustained improvement in the cycle as a strategic result, since it raises both returns and the growth ceiling.

body.label: Check cash conversion for any listed company
body.description: Take Cash from Operating Activity from the Cash Flow section and divide it by Operating Profit from the Profit and Loss section, for each of the last five years. A company whose ratio keeps falling while profit rises is worth a much closer look.

body.text: A rupee released from working capital is worth more than a rupee of extra profit. It arrives as cash, it needs no new sales, it lowers the capital the business runs on, and it raises how fast that business can grow.

points: Working capital sits in the denominator of ROCE, so two companies with identical profit can report returns several points apart.
In the worked example, running working capital at 15% of sales rather than 30% was worth 6.7 percentage points of ROCE.
Working capital intensity sets the self-funded growth rate, and a leaner cycle raises the speed limit on growth.
An increase in working capital is subtracted directly in free cash flow, so a profitable growing company can generate nothing for its owners.
A permanent improvement creates value twice: a one-time cash release, and lower cash absorption in every future year.
Multiples based on EBITDA do not see working capital, but net debt and the normalised working capital adjustment in a deal do.
Cash conversion, that is operating cash flow divided by operating profit, is the fastest test of whether reported profit is arriving as cash.
